questions.question: Which description of how R represents a matrix such as `matrix(1:6, nrow = 2)` is correct?
options: A list of 3 column vectors of equal length, each of which may have its own type.
An atomic vector of 6 values with a dimension attribute: 2 rows, 3 columns.
Two separate row vectors of length 3, stored one after the other under one name.
A two-dimensional table that can hold numbers only, so text cannot be stored in it.

questions.question: Which values form the second column of the matrix created by `matrix(1:8, nrow = 2)`?
What does `dim(c(4, 5, 6))` return?
options: `NULL`

questions.question: With `x <- c(2, 5, 9)` and `y <- c(7, 1, 4)`, which call creates a 3-by-2 matrix whose columns are `x` and `y`?
options: `rbind(x, y)`
`matrix(c(x, y), nrow = 2)`
`cbind(x, y)`

questions.question: With `x <- c(2, 5, 9)` and `y <- c(7, 1, 4)`, what does `rownames(cbind(x, y))` return?
options: `NULL`

questions.question: Which call creates the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\end{pmatrix}$ in R?
options: `matrix(1:6, nrow = 2)`
`matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)`
`matrix(1:6, ncol = 2, byrow = TRUE)`
`matrix(c(1, 4, 2, 5, 3, 6), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)`

questions.question: `matrix(1:7, nrow = 3)` prints the warning `data length [7] is not a sub-multiple or multiple of the number of rows [3]`. What has R done?
options: It created a 3-by-3 matrix and filled the last two cells with `1` and `2` again.
It stopped, so no matrix was created and nothing was printed apart from the message.
It created a 3-by-3 matrix and left `NA` in the two cells that had no value.
It created a 3-by-2 matrix and dropped the seventh value to make the data fit.

questions.question: What happens to the ages in `cbind(c(19, 22), c("Ann", "Bo"))`?
options: They stay numbers, because each column of a matrix keeps the type of its vector.
R stops with an error, because a matrix cannot combine numbers with text.
They become the strings `"19"` and `"22"`: a matrix has one type for all cells.
They become `NA`, because numbers cannot be stored in a character matrix.

questions.question: For two numeric vectors `x` and `y` of length 3, how are `rbind(x, y)` and `cbind(x, y)` related?
options: They are the same 2-by-3 matrix; only the printed layout of the two results differs.
They have the same dimensions, but the values of `x` and `y` appear in a different order.
They are unrelated, because `cbind()` fills its result row by row and `rbind()` column by column.
They hold the same numbers with rows and columns swapped: each is the transpose of the other.

questions.question: Which values form the second column of `matrix(c(4, 8, 1, 6, 2, 9), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)`?
In R 4.x, what does `class(cbind(c(1, 2), c(3, 4)))` return?
options: `[1] "matrix" "array"`
`[1] "numeric"`
`[1] "data.frame"`
`[1] "matrix"`

questions.question: Which call creates the same matrix as `matrix(1:6, nrow = 2)`?
options: `matrix(1:6, ncol = 2)`
`matrix(1:6, ncol = 3)`

questions.question: After `A <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE); B <- matrix(A, nrow = 3)`, what does `B[1, 2]` return?
options: It stops with an error, since `A` is already a matrix.

questions.question: After `M <- matrix(c(5, 1, 8, 2, 7, 3), nrow = 2)`, what happens when R runs `rownames(M) <- c("a", "b", "c")`?
options: The rows are named `"a"` and `"b"`, and `"c"` is dropped with a warning.
The three names go on the columns instead, since `M` has three columns.
It stops with an error, because `M` has 2 rows and 3 names were given.
The three rows are named `"a"`, `"b"` and `"c"`, without any message.
